# II. The Fiduciary Floor

Delaware courts have long treated the duty of loyalty as the floor beneath every board decision.[^1] That floor reaches controllers who stand on both sides of a transaction.[^2] The entire-fairness standard follows from it.[^3] A controller can shift the burden only by conditioning the deal on both protections at the outset.[^4] Without them, the court reviews the price itself.[^5]

[^1]: Guth v. Loft, Inc., 5 A.2d 503, 510 (Del. 1939).
[^2]: Weinberger v. UOP, Inc., 457 A.2d 701, 710 (Del. 1983) (citing Guth, 5 A.2d at 510).
[^3]: Id. at 711.
[^4]: Kahn v. M & F Worldwide Corp., 88 A.3d 635, 644 (Del. 2014). The court framed the two protections as a package. Id. at 645.
[^5]: Weinberger, 457 A.2d at 711.
